TLDR: Importing a used car to Argentina requires AFIP customs declaration, paying 35% import duty plus additional taxes, obtaining CNRT approval, and completing vehicle registration with DNRPA. The process typically takes 30-45 days and costs 50-70% of the vehicle's value in total fees.

How to Import a Used Car to Argentina: Complete Process Overview

Importing a used car to Argentina involves navigating the AFIP (Federal Administration of Public Revenue) customs system, paying substantial import duties, and completing vehicle registration through DNRPA (National Registry of Motor Property). The process requires careful documentation, significant financial investment, and compliance with strict Argentine automotive import regulations established in 2026.

Argentine customs law permits used vehicle imports under specific conditions, with vehicles older than 10 years prohibited from importation. The total cost typically ranges from 50-70% of the vehicle's declared value when including all duties, taxes, and processing fees. Most imports enter through Puerto de Buenos Aires or Puerto Dock Sud, Argentina's primary automotive clearance facilities.

As a Vehicle Export Specialist at RosM Autos, I have assisted numerous clients with Argentine vehicle imports since 2018. Our experience shows that proper documentation and accurate valuation are critical for smooth customs clearance, with preparation time significantly impacting overall import costs and timeline.

AFIP Customs Requirements and Documentation

AFIP requires a comprehensive documentation package for used vehicle imports, including the original vehicle title, export certificate from the origin country, commercial invoice, bill of lading, and CUIT/CUIL taxpayer identification. The importer must be registered as an Argentine taxpayer or work through a licensed customs broker with AFIP authorization.

The primary documentation checklist includes:

  • Original vehicle title or equivalent ownership document
  • Export certificate issued by origin country customs
  • Commercial invoice with detailed vehicle specifications
  • Bill of lading from shipping company
  • Certificate of origin (Form A for preferential duty treatment)
  • Vehicle inspection certificate confirming roadworthiness
  • Insurance policy covering the import period
  • AFIP customs declaration (SIMI system)

Vehicle specifications must match exactly across all documents. Any discrepancies in VIN numbers, engine specifications, or model details will trigger customs inspection delays. RosM Autos provides comprehensive export documentation services, ensuring all paperwork meets AFIP requirements before shipment to minimize clearance complications.

SIMI System Registration Process

The SIMI (Integral Import Monitoring System) requires advance registration before vehicle shipment. Importers must submit detailed vehicle information, including manufacturer, model year, engine type, fuel system, and emissions compliance data. SIMI approval typically takes 5-10 business days and costs approximately $200 USD in processing fees.

CNRT (National Commission for Transport Regulation) approval is mandatory for all vehicle imports. This process verifies the vehicle meets Argentine safety and emissions standards, with inspections conducted at authorized facilities in Buenos Aires or surrounding provinces.

Argentina Car Import Duty Rates and Tax Structure

Argentina imposes a 35% import duty on used vehicles, calculated on the vehicle's FOB (Free on Board) value plus shipping costs. Additional taxes include 21% IVA (Value Added Tax), 0.5% statistical tax, and various port handling fees that typically add another 8-12% to the total cost structure.

The complete tax breakdown for 2026 includes:

Import Duty35%CIF Value
IVA (VAT)21%CIF + Import Duty

Port Fees8-12%Variable
Customs Broker$800-1200Fixed Fee

According to INDEC (National Institute of Statistics and Census), vehicle import duties generated $2.3 billion in revenue for Argentina in 2025, with used vehicle imports representing approximately 15% of this total. The high tax structure aims to protect domestic automotive manufacturing while generating government revenue.

Preferential duty rates apply to vehicles from MERCOSUR countries (Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay), reducing the base import duty to 20%. However, vehicles must meet strict origin requirements, with at least 60% of components manufactured within MERCOSUR territory to qualify for preferential treatment.

Valuation Methods and Customs Assessment

AFIP uses the transaction value method for customs valuation, requiring detailed commercial invoices with itemized costs. Customs officials may reject declared values deemed too low, substituting reference prices based on similar vehicle sales data from international automotive databases.

The National Customs Authority maintains a database of reference values for common vehicle models, updated quarterly based on international market data. Declared values more than 15% below reference prices trigger automatic inspection and potential valuation adjustment, adding 10-20 days to the clearance process.

Buenos Aires Port Clearance Procedures

Puerto de Buenos Aires handles approximately 70% of Argentine vehicle imports, with Puerto Dock Sud processing most container shipments. Vehicle clearance requires physical inspection by customs officials, typically conducted at Terminal 4 (Puerto Nuevo) or the specialized automotive facility at Dock Sud.

The port clearance process follows this timeline:

  1. Arrival Notification (Day 1-2): Shipping agent notifies customs of vehicle arrival
  2. Documentation Review (Day 3-5): AFIP reviews all import documents
  3. Physical Inspection (Day 6-8): Customs examines vehicle condition and specifications
  4. Duty Assessment (Day 9-10): Final calculation of all taxes and fees
  5. Payment Processing (Day 11-12): Payment of duties through AFIP system
  6. Release Authorization (Day 13-15): Vehicle cleared for domestic transport

Port storage fees accrue daily after the 10-day free period, typically costing $25-35 per day for standard vehicles. Expedited clearance services are available for an additional $300-500 fee, reducing processing time by 3-5 days.

Terminal operating hours run Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM, with limited Saturday operations for urgent clearances. Vehicle pickup requires authorized transport companies with proper insurance coverage and CNRT registration for automotive cargo handling.

Customs Inspection Requirements

Physical inspection verifies vehicle condition, mileage accuracy, and compliance with declared specifications. Inspectors check VIN numbers, engine codes, emission control systems, and safety equipment against import documentation. Any modifications or damage not declared on shipping documents may result in additional duties or clearance delays.

Approximately 25% of used vehicle imports undergo comprehensive inspection, according to 2025 AFIP statistics. Factors triggering detailed inspection include first-time importers, high-value vehicles over $50,000, or vehicles from countries with limited automotive export controls.

Vehicle Registration with DNRPA

The National Registry of Motor Property (DNRPA) handles vehicle registration after customs clearance. Registration requires proof of customs duty payment, vehicle insurance, technical inspection certificate, and completion of Form 08 (Vehicle Registration Application). The process typically takes 15-20 business days and costs approximately $150-200 in administrative fees.

Required documentation for DNRPA registration includes:

  • AFIP customs clearance certificate
  • Proof of duty and tax payment
  • Certificate of technical inspection (RTO)
  • Compulsory insurance policy
  • Proof of Argentine residence or legal status
  • Completed Form 08 with notarized signatures

Technical inspection (Revisión Técnica Obligatoria - RTO) must be completed at authorized facilities within 30 days of customs clearance. The inspection verifies emissions compliance, safety systems, and roadworthiness according to Argentine automotive standards. RTO certificates are valid for one year for vehicles under 3 years old, with more frequent inspections required for older vehicles.

License plates are issued by provincial authorities, with Buenos Aires Province handling the majority of imported vehicle registrations. Plate issuance typically takes 5-7 business days after DNRPA registration completion, with temporary permits available for immediate use.

Provincial Registration Variations

Each Argentine province maintains specific registration requirements, with some variations in documentation and fees. Córdoba Province, for example, requires additional environmental impact declarations for vehicles over 3.0-liter engine displacement, while Mendoza Province mandates Spanish translation of all foreign documents by certified translators.

Registration transfer between provinces requires updated insurance coverage, new technical inspections, and payment of provincial transfer taxes ranging from $100-300 depending on vehicle value and destination province.

Import Restrictions and Prohibited Vehicles

Argentina prohibits importation of vehicles older than 10 years from manufacturing date, with strict enforcement through VIN number verification and manufacturing documentation review. Right-hand drive vehicles are prohibited except for specific commercial applications with CNRT authorization. Vehicles lacking proper emission control systems or safety equipment cannot obtain import approval.

Prohibited vehicle categories include:

  • Vehicles manufactured before 2016 (as of 2026)
  • Right-hand drive passenger vehicles
  • Vehicles without catalytic converters
  • Reconstructed or salvage title vehicles
  • Vehicles lacking airbag systems
  • Motorcycles over 600cc (restricted import quotas)

CNRT maintains updated lists of approved vehicle models, manufacturers, and specifications. Vehicles not appearing on approved lists require individual evaluation and certification, adding 30-60 days to the import process and costing an additional $500-1000 in evaluation fees.

Commercial vehicles, including trucks and buses, face additional restrictions based on weight, passenger capacity, and intended use. Professional transport vehicles require commercial operator licenses and compliance with specific safety and maintenance standards.

Environmental and Safety Compliance

Euro 4 emission standards are mandatory for all imported vehicles, with Euro 5 requirements taking effect in January 2027. Vehicles must demonstrate compliance through manufacturer certificates or independent testing at approved facilities. Non-compliant vehicles face rejection or costly modification requirements before registration approval.

Safety equipment requirements include dual front airbags, ABS braking systems, and electronic stability control for vehicles manufactured after 2018. Retrofit installation of required safety equipment is permitted but must be completed by certified automotive technicians with proper documentation.

Cost Analysis and Financial Planning

Total import costs for a $20,000 USD vehicle typically range from $32,000-36,000 USD when including all duties, taxes, shipping, and administrative fees. This represents a 60-80% markup over the original purchase price, making careful financial planning essential for potential importers.

Currency fluctuations significantly impact import costs, with the Argentine peso's volatility affecting final payment amounts. Most importers hedge currency risk through forward contracts or payment in stable currencies where permitted by AFIP regulations.

Financing options include bank letters of credit, import financing programs, and specialized automotive import loans offered by select Argentine financial institutions. Interest rates typically range from 18-25% annually for import financing, with repayment terms up to 36 months.

Insurance and Protection Strategies

Comprehensive insurance coverage is mandatory during the import process, protecting against shipping damage, theft, and customs-related losses. Marine cargo insurance typically costs 0.5-1.0% of vehicle value, with higher rates for luxury or high-performance vehicles.

Import duty insurance protects against valuation disputes and additional assessments, covering potential cost overruns up to 25% of declared duties. This specialized coverage costs approximately 2-3% of estimated duty amounts but provides valuable protection against customs valuation adjustments.

Timeline and Process Management

The complete import process typically requires 45-60 days from vehicle purchase to domestic registration, with variations based on origin country, documentation quality, and customs processing volumes. Peak import periods (November-February) may extend timelines due to increased cargo volumes at Buenos Aires ports.

Typical timeline breakdown:

  1. Pre-import Documentation (5-10 days): SIMI registration, CNRT approval, document preparation
  2. Shipping Transit (15-25 days): Ocean freight from origin port to Buenos Aires
  3. Customs Clearance (10-15 days): AFIP processing, inspection, duty payment
  4. Vehicle Registration (15-20 days): DNRPA processing, technical inspection, plate issuance

Expedited processing options are available for time-sensitive imports, including priority customs clearance and accelerated registration services. These services typically add 15-25% to standard processing fees but can reduce total timeline by 10-15 days.

Effective communication with customs brokers, shipping agents, and registration officials is crucial for maintaining import timeline momentum. Regular status updates and proactive document management significantly improve processing efficiency and reduce potential delays.

Common Delays and Solutions

Documentation discrepancies represent the most common cause of import delays, accounting for approximately 40% of extended clearance times according to Buenos Aires Port Authority statistics. Complete document review before shipment eliminates most preventable delays and associated storage costs.

Currency availability for duty payments can cause processing delays during periods of foreign exchange restrictions. Maintaining adequate peso reserves or securing approved foreign currency sources ensures timely payment capability when customs clearance is completed.

Professional Services and Support

Licensed customs brokers are mandatory for vehicle imports exceeding $5,000 USD in value, with brokers handling AFIP interactions, duty calculations, and clearance procedures. Broker fees typically range from $800-1200 USD, depending on vehicle value and complexity of the import process.

faqItems.question: How much does it cost to import a used car to Argentina?
faqItems.answer: Total import costs typically range from 60-80% of the vehicle's purchase price. This includes 35% import duty, 21% VAT, shipping costs ($2,000-3,000), port fees, and administrative expenses. For a $20,000 vehicle, expect total costs of $32,000-36,000.

faqItems.question: What vehicles cannot be imported to Argentina?
faqItems.answer: Argentina prohibits vehicles older than 10 years (manufactured before 2016 as of 2026), right-hand drive passenger cars, vehicles without catalytic converters, salvage title vehicles, cars lacking airbag systems, and motorcycles over 600cc without special permits.

faqItems.question: How long does the Argentine car import process take?
faqItems.answer: The complete process requires 45-60 days from purchase to registration. This includes 5-10 days for pre-import documentation, 15-25 days shipping, 10-15 days customs clearance, and 15-20 days for vehicle registration with DNRPA.

faqItems.question: Do I need a customs broker to import a car to Argentina?
faqItems.answer: Yes, licensed customs brokers are mandatory for vehicle imports exceeding $5,000 USD. Brokers handle AFIP interactions, duty calculations, and clearance procedures. Fees typically range from $800-1,200 USD depending on vehicle value and complexity.

faqItems.question: What documents are required for Argentine vehicle import?
faqItems.answer: Required documents include original vehicle title, export certificate, commercial invoice, bill of lading, certificate of origin, vehicle inspection certificate, insurance policy, and AFIP customs declaration through the SIMI system. All specifications must match exactly across documents.
